q: Which company is a major local supplier of long-span roofing and steel decking?
n: Dwightsteel Building Systems is a major local supplier of long-span roofing and steel decking. Source: Dwightsteel (company site).

q: Which of the following is a local steel manufacturer?
n: SteelAsia is a Philippine steel manufacturer. SteelAsia produces reinforcing bars and structural sections in several plants across the country. Source: SteelAsia (official site).

q: Which company is known for producing galvanized iron (GI) sheets and roofing materials in the Philippines?
n: Puyat Steel Corporation produces galvanized iron sheets and roofing materials in the Philippines. Source: Puyat Steel (company site).

q: What is commonly produced through a continuous process of cold-rolling and hot-rolling steel?
n: Continuous hot- and cold-rolling turns steel into a wide variety of products: bars, sections, sheets and coils. Source: World Steel Association; ASTM A6.

q: An ASTM #3 bar has a diameter of about:
n: An ASTM #3 bar is 3/8 in. (≈9.5 mm) in diameter, roughly a 10 mm bar. US bar numbers give the diameter in eighths of an inch, so #3 = 3/8 in. Source: ASTM A615.

q: What is the standard commercial length of deformed bars?
n: Deformed bars are commonly sold in 6 m commercial lengths, with longer lengths by order. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; PNS 49.

q: Which element mainly governs the ductility of steel?
n: Carbon content mainly governs steel's ductility. More carbon raises strength and lowers ductility. Source: ASTM A6; Callister, Materials Science and Engineering.

q: What is an advantage of steel over concrete?
n: Steel's advantage over concrete here is elasticity: it deforms and recovers under load, with high tensile strength and ductility. Source: Callister, Materials Science and Engineering; AISC.

q: Which beam best resists twisting under torsion?
n: Closed sections such as box beams resist torsion best. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: What steel section is commonly used for skylight installations?
n: Tubular hollow structural sections (HSS) are the usual framing for skylights. Source: AISC HSS Connections Manual; glazing manufacturer data.

q: What steel section is typically used for exposed structural frameworks?
n: Exposed structural frameworks typically use tubular (hollow) sections. Their clean shape and torsional stiffness suit architecturally exposed steel. Source: AISC Code of Standard Practice, Sec. 10 (AESS); AISC HSS Connections Manual.

q: In steel terms, HSS stands for:
n: HSS means Hollow Structural Section (square, rectangular or round tubes). Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual; ASTM A500.

q: Which prestressing method tensions the tendons before concrete is placed?
n: Pre-tensioning tensions the tendons before the concrete is placed, then releases them once it has hardened. It is common in precast plants. Source: PCI Design Handbook; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4.

q: Which prestressing method tensions tendons after the concrete has gained strength?
n: Post-tensioning tensions tendons in ducts after the concrete has gained strength, then anchors them. Source: Post-Tensioning Institute; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4.

q: What are the wires or strands used in post-tensioning called?
n: The wires or strands used in post-tensioning are called tendons. Tendons are high-strength steel wires, strands or bars that apply precompression to the concrete. Source: Post-Tensioning Institute.

q: What is the main advantage of prestressed over ordinary reinforced concrete?
n: Precompression gives prestressed concrete higher capacity, longer spans and better crack control than ordinary RC. Source: PCI Design Handbook; Lin & Burns, Design of Prestressed Concrete Structures.

q: What anchors tendons in post-tensioned concrete?
n: Tendons are anchored at their ends by anchor heads with wedges, bearing on anchor plates. Source: Post-Tensioning Institute.

q: What typically happens to steel when subjected to stress?
n: Steel is ductile. Stressed past yield it bends and deforms plastically rather than breaking suddenly. Source: Callister, Materials Science and Engineering; AISC.

q: What usually occurs to the steel reinforcement in a slab or concrete beam as the structural member nears failure?
n: In an under-reinforced member near failure, the steel yields and the member deflects visibly before collapse, which is the ductile warning. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 421.2.2 (tension-controlled sections).

q: What does a 6 m, 10 mm deformed bar weigh?
n: A 10 mm bar weighs 0.617 kg/m, so a 6 m bar weighs 0.617 × 6 = 3.70 kg. Source: PNS 49; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (bar weights).

q: What does a 6 m, 12 mm deformed bar weigh?
n: A 12 mm bar weighs 0.888 kg/m, so a 6 m bar weighs 5.33 kg. Bar unit weight is d²/162 kg/m (d in mm), so 12²/162 = 0.888 kg/m. Source: PNS 49; Fajardo.

q: What does a 6 m, 16 mm deformed bar weigh?
n: A 16 mm bar weighs 1.578 kg/m, so a 6 m bar weighs 9.47 kg. Using d²/162 kg/m: 16²/162 = 1.580 kg/m, so a 6 m bar weighs about 9.47 kg. Source: PNS 49; Fajardo.

q: What is the minimum yield strength of Grade 40 rebar?
n: Grade 40 rebar has a minimum yield strength of 40,000 psi (≈280 MPa). The grade number gives the minimum yield strength in ksi, and Grade 40 bars are suited to light construction. Source: ASTM A615.

q: What is the minimum tensile strength of Grade 40 rebar?
n: Grade 40 rebar has a minimum tensile strength of 60,000 psi. The required tensile strength (60 ksi) is higher than the yield (40 ksi), which gives ductility. Source: ASTM A615, Table 2.

q: What is the minimum yield strength of Grade 60 rebar?
n: Grade 60 rebar has a minimum yield strength of 60,000 psi (≈420 MPa). Grade 60 is the common structural grade for beams, columns and footings. Source: ASTM A615.

q: What is the minimum tensile strength of Grade 60 rebar?
n: Grade 60 rebar has a minimum tensile strength of 90,000 psi. The required tensile strength (90 ksi) is well above the 60 ksi yield, giving the ductility needed for seismic design. Source: ASTM A615, Table 2.

q: What is the minimum size of reinforcing bars used for footings?
n: Footing reinforcement is commonly at least 12 mm bars. Source: Philippine detailing practice; NSCP 2015, Sec. 413.

q: What is the minimum size of reinforcing bars used for slab-on-fill?
n: Slabs on fill are commonly reinforced with at least 10 mm bars (or welded mesh). Source: Philippine detailing practice; ACI 360R.

q: A standard 90° hook needs an extension at the free end of:
n: A standard 90° hook on a main bar needs a 12db extension at its free end. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 425.3.1.

q: The clear spacing between parallel bars in a layer must be at least db and not less than:
n: Clear spacing between parallel bars in a layer must be at least db and at least 25 mm. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 425.2.1.

q: The standard hook for stirrups and ties shall be:
n: NSCP permits all three stirrup and tie hooks: 90° + 6db (16 mm bars and smaller), 90° + 12db (20–25 mm bars), and 135° + 6db (25 mm bars and smaller). Source: NSCP 2015, Table 425.3.2.

q: In spiral or tied columns, the minimum clear spacing between longitudinal bars is:
n: In columns, clear spacing between longitudinal bars must be at least 1.5db and at least 40 mm. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 425.2.3.

q: Bars larger than what size may not be bundled in beams?
n: Bars larger than 36 mm may not be bundled in beams. The limit keeps bundles small enough for proper bond and concrete placement. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 425.6.1.

q: Astandard hook may consist of a 180-degree bend plus a 4 db extension at the free end of not less than ___ mm.
n: A standard hook may be a 180° bend plus a 4db extension, but not less than 60 mm, at the free end. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 425.3.1.

q: What is the minimum cover for footing bars cast against earth?
n: Footings cast against earth need 75 mm cover. The thick cover protects the bars from soil moisture and corrosion, since such surfaces are not formed. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1.
